newsitem.title: USA: New York special session seen only lasting one day.
newsitem.headline: New York special session seen only lasting one day.

text.p: New York State's special session might be as short as one day, but the final agenda will not be finalized until a meeting between the leaders set to begin early tonight, legislative officials said Monday.
Much of the impetus for a short session appeared to be coming from Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno (R-Troy). "Right now, we anticipate it being just one day," said a spokeswoman for Bruno.

Gov. George Pataki, as expected, last week called for the special session to begin on Tuesday, and to take up reforming how New York City's schools are run, extending New York City's personal income tax surcharge and commuter transit taxes paid by 12 downstate counties, and the current bank tax structure.

But the Democrat-led Assembly's desire to include school-based budgeting in reforming how New York City's schools are governed was opposed by the Senate, a legislative source, who declined to be named, said.

He explained that the Senate, which is controlled by Republicans, evidently did not think it necessary to impose this requirement with legislation, though it agreed the proposal had merit. "If the Assembly dropped that as a demand, the bill would go," one said.

New York City likely will have to wait until the legislature reconvenes in January for it to take up its proposal to create a new infrastructure finance authority, as well as an alternative emergency authority proposed by Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver.

"There are still a number of outstanding issues to be resolved," said the legislative source, citing questions about the state constitution, local finance laws and capital finance. The city says it needs a new bonding authority to sidestep its consititutional debt limit, which it is expected to hit late in its 1997 fiscal year, which ends on June 30.
The city's debt cap, calculated on a five-year average of real estate values, has fallen sharply because prices were eroded by the severe local recession in the early 1990s.
